questions.q: Define market demand and state the mathematical operation used to derive it from individual demands.
questions.a: Market demand is the total quantity of a good all consumers in a market are willing and able to purchase at each price, derived by horizontally summing (adding quantities at each price) individual demand schedules. A wrong answer that says "vertically summing prices" or "averaging individual demands" reveals confusion between horizontal summation (quantities) and vertical summation (prices), a fundamental error in demand aggregation.

questions.q: Explain why the market demand curve is flatter (more price-elastic) than any individual demand curve, even when all individuals have identical demand curves.
questions.a: Because market demand adds quantities horizontally, a given price change triggers a larger total quantity response across many consumers than for a single consumer. A wrong answer claiming "market demand is steeper because more people buy" confuses the direction of elasticity: more buyers amplify quantity response, making the curve flatter, not steeper.

questions.q:
Three consumers — A, B, and C — have individual demand schedules for mangoes (kg) at prices ₹50, ₹40, ₹30, ₹20, ₹10 per kg:
A: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10
B: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5
C: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4
Construct the market demand schedule and calculate the total market quantity demanded at ₹30/kg.
questions.a: Step 1: Align prices and quantities. Step 2: At ₹30/kg, A demands 6 kg, B demands 3 kg, C demands 2 kg. Step 3: Horizontal sum = 6 + 3 + 2 = 11 kg. Step 4: Full market schedule at ₹50,₹40,₹30,₹20,₹10: 3, 7, 11, 15, 19 kg. A wrong answer of 11 kg but with incorrect schedule (e.g., averaging) shows mechanical addition without understanding the price-quantity correspondence.

questions.q: In a village market, 50 households each have identical demand for wheat: Qd = 10 - 0.5P. If 20 households migrate to the city, how does the market demand curve change? Describe the shift and its economic implication for the wheat seller.
questions.a: Original market demand: Qd_market = 50*(10 - 0.5P) = 500 - 25P. After migration: Qd_market = 30*(10 - 0.5P) = 300 - 15P. The curve shifts left (decreases) and becomes steeper (less elastic) because fewer buyers reduce total quantity at every price and reduce responsiveness. A wrong answer saying "curve shifts right" or "becomes flatter" reveals misunderstanding that fewer buyers shrink and steepen market demand.

questions.q: A textbook states: "Market demand is simply the demand of the average consumer multiplied by the number of consumers." Evaluate this statement. Is it always true? Provide a counterexample if false.
questions.a: False. This only holds if all consumers have identical demand curves. Counterexample: Two consumers, one demands 10 units at ₹10, another demands 0 units at ₹10. Average demand = 5 units, multiplied by 2 = 10 units. But true horizontal sum = 10 + 0 = 10 units (coincidentally same here). Better: at ₹5, first demands 15, second demands 5. Average = 10, ×2 = 20. Horizontal sum = 15+5=20. Actually works for linear identical? Wait, if demands are different shapes, average × N ≠ horizontal sum. Example: Consumer 1: Q=20-P, Consumer 2: Q=10-0.5P. At P=5, Q1=15, Q2=7.5, sum=22.5. Average demand = (30-1.5P)/2 = 15-0.75P, at P=5 gives 11.25, ×2=22.5. Actually for linear demands, average × N = horizontal sum because summation is linear. The statement is mathematically true for linear demands but conceptually misleading because it hides the horizontal summation process. The error is pedagogical: it encourages vertical thinking. A wrong answer saying "always true" misses the conceptual distinction between averaging and horizontal addition.

questions.q: Create a real-world scenario in an Indian weekly haat (market) where three types of buyers (a restaurant owner, a household, and a street vendor) have different demand schedules for onions. Draw the individual and market demand curves on graph paper, labeling axes, and explain why the market curve is flatter.
questions.a: A good answer provides a table with three distinct demand schedules (e.g., restaurant buys 50kg at ₹20, household 5kg, vendor 10kg), correctly plots quantity on x-axis and price on y-axis, draws three downward-sloping individual curves, then a market curve that lies to the right and is flatter. Explanation: horizontal addition of quantities at each price makes market quantity more responsive. A poor answer draws vertical summation or identical curves, showing confusion between individual and market perspectives.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: ______ demand is the quantity of a good a single consumer is willing and able to buy at each possible price during a given period, ceteris paribus.
Fill in the blank: Imagine you visit a vegetable ______ in Mumbai and see three buyers — Ramesh, Sunita, and Arjun — each deciding how many kilograms of tomatoes to buy at ₹40/kg.
What is Individual demand? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Individual demand is the quantity of a good a single consumer is willing and able to buy at each possible price during a given period, ceteris paribus.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Imagine you visit a vegetable market in Mumbai and see three buyers — Ramesh, Sunita, and Arjun — each deciding how many kilograms of tomatoes to buy at ₹______/kg.
What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Individual demand?
questions.a: Students believe market demand is found by vertically adding individual demand curves (adding prices at each quantity) because they confuse "adding demand" with "adding supply" (where market supply is horizontal summation too, but they misremember).

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can construct a market demand schedule from individual demand schedules by horizontally summing quantities at each price, and explain why market demand is more elastic than any single individual's demand.
